patch.value: The ordering graph is flat: 1763 of 1991 sequenced nodes have no predecessor and the critical path is 6, so every scheduling analytic describes a workspace that barely has an order

Measured 2026-07-27. pm graph analyze reports node_count 2121 and edge_count 9262 over a fully connected corpus, component_count 1 and orphan_count 0, which is a genuine achievement of the terminal backfill. The ordering layer underneath it is a different story. Of those 9262 edges only 601 express sequence: blocked_by 383 and blocks 218, or 6.5 percent. Everything else is hierarchy or association: parent 1943, child 15, implements 1973, related 4437, verifies 129, discovered_from 161, incident_from 2, supersedes 1. The consequence is reported directly by the analyzer: layer_count 7, critical_path_length 6, and frontier_count 1763 out of ordered_node_count 1991, so 88.5 percent of sequenced nodes have no predecessor at all. Every analytic that consumes the ordering DAG therefore describes a nearly flat structure regardless of how much history the workspace holds. The critical path names six items out of two thousand. Slack, dominators and layering are computed over a shape that is one hub and a wide flat rim, with pm-mpbb at degree 209. Readiness in pm next is trivially satisfiable because almost nothing has an unmet predecessor. This is not the same gap as the reachability invariant, which asks whether every item reaches an outcome milestone within a bounded number of hops and therefore constrains paths from above. This asks the opposite question and finds the structure degenerate from below: the corpus records what work belongs to what, and almost never what had to happen before what. Because the ordering edges are the ones that carry time, the project timeline is the part of the graph that traversal cannot recover.

Ordering-graph shape is a reported profile in its own right: predecessor coverage, layer distribution, and longest-path length are measured and trended, not implied by a critical path sample; A stated policy distinguishes items that legitimately have no predecessor from items whose predecessor was simply never recorded, so the frontier count becomes interpretable; Sequencing edges recovered for terminal work come from durable evidence such as history instants, release boundaries, shared artefacts and explicit references, and ambiguity is retained rather than resolved by fabrication; Scheduling analytics declare the fraction of the corpus they actually order, so a critical path over 6 of 2121 nodes is never presented as a workspace-wide result; The profile stays inside the graph analytics token and latency budgets and remains bounded at million-item scale
Make the project timeline recoverable by traversal, so graph algorithms can reconstruct what preceded what and not only what belongs to what
A connected graph that cannot order itself answers structural questions but not historical ones; ordering edges are what turn the tracker into a timeline
Critical path, slack, dominators and readiness all currently describe a 6-deep DAG and will keep doing so at any corpus size
The terminal backfill closed the connectivity gap and made this the next visible one: 100 percent of nodes are reachable and 88.5 percent of them have no predecessor
pm 2026.7.27, this workspace at 2118 items, measured via pm graph analyze --json and pm graph audit --summary

Run pm graph analyze --json and read execution.frontier_count against execution.ordered_node_count and execution.critical_path_length; cross-check edge composition with pm graph audit --summary and read profile.edges_by_kind
Longest-path depth and predecessor coverage grow with the recorded history of the project
critical_path_length 6, layer_count 7, frontier_count 1763 of 1991, and 6.5 percent of edges carry sequence

message: File the degenerate ordering graph found while profiling relationship depth

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Evidence 2026-07-27: the reported critical path is not a work sequence, it is a duplicate cluster.

pm graph analyze returns execution.critical_path as pm-phpq, pm-204c, pm-iziy, pm-f0e9, pm-mn6w, pm-wjdr, pm-a5ea. Reading those seven items shows what the chain actually is. They are titled Release-readiness maintenance loop 2026-03-07 run 2, run 3, and so on: a set of near-identical items produced by a repeating maintenance loop on a single day in March 2026. Their own history records the relationship explicitly. Each of the trailing six carries a comment written on 2026-04-04 by a dedupe pass reading, verbatim, that this item is superseded by pm-phpq for cluster release-loop::2026-03-07.

So the longest path the analyzer can find through this workspace is six hops of duplicate consolidation. The edges that carry it are related edges, all created at one instant on 2026-07-26 by the terminal-history backfill, which is exactly the right thing for that backfill to have recorded and exactly the wrong thing to present as a critical path. The analytic is not wrong about the graph; the graph does not contain a longer chain of anything else.

Two consequences worth separating.

The first is that the depth deficit this item describes is worse than the raw number suggests. A critical path of six sounds shallow; a critical path of six that turns out to be one item and five copies of it means the true longest sequence of causally ordered work in a two-thousand-item corpus spanning months is shorter than six. There is no ordered spine at all, only a wide flat rim and one hub.

The second is a concrete remediation that costs nothing to justify, because the evidence is machine-written and unambiguous. Those duplicate-consolidation relationships are supersedes, not related. Retyping them removes fabricated ordering signal from the execution DAG at the same time as it makes the consolidation lineage traversable, so it improves both halves of the problem with one change and no judgement call. A first tranche of this was applied on 2026-07-27 under the evidence rules in pm-lnrk: 39 supersedes edges recovered from durable text, taking the kind from 1 edge to 40 across the corpus. The remaining work is not more extraction, it is deciding whether the analyzer should treat related as an ordering edge at all, which is the question this item and pm-4020c5 meet on.

value.text:
Correction and new evidence, 2026-07-27 (second look at the reported critical path).

The existing note on this item states that the edges carrying the reported critical path were "all created at one instant on 2026-07-26 by the terminal-history backfill". The item files contradict that. Reading the dependency rows directly:

  pm-204c -> pm-phpq  related  2026-03-07T07:48:09Z  author maintainer-agent
  pm-iziy -> pm-204c  related  2026-03-07T08:03:43Z  author maintainer-agent
  pm-f0e9 -> pm-iziy  related  2026-03-07T08:20:06Z  author maintainer-agent
  pm-mn6w -> pm-f0e9  related  2026-03-07T09:31:15Z  author maintainer-agent
  pm-wjdr -> pm-mn6w  related  2026-03-07T09:48:11Z  author maintainer-agent
  pm-a5ea -> pm-wjdr  related  2026-03-07T10:12:40Z  author maintainer-agent

Six of the seven chain edges were written live on 2026-03-07, each run linking to the run before it, minutes apart, by the agent that was executing the loop. Only the hub edges (every run also pointing at pm-phpq) came from the 2026-07-26 backfill, at 17:00-17:28 that day.

This changes the conclusion. The longest path in this workspace is not an artefact of a backfill and it is not six copies of one item. It is a real sequential record: runs 2 through 8 of a release-readiness maintenance loop, executed in that order on one morning, with each step recording its predecessor at the moment it happened. It is the only genuinely ordered chain the corpus contains, and it was recorded by an agent that simply wrote down what came before. The depth deficit is therefore not that the project never had order; it is that this discipline was applied on one day in March and essentially never again.

The second finding is an ambiguity that must be retained rather than resolved, and it is exactly the case this item's third acceptance criterion anticipates. Two durable records disagree about the direction of the same relationship. The 2026-03-07 edges say run N+1 follows run N, so the sequence runs phpq, 204c, iziy, f0e9, mn6w, wjdr, a5ea. The machine-written 2026-04-04 dedupe comments say each of the trailing runs is superseded by pm-phpq, and supersedes read as an ordering kind places the superseded item before its replacement, which reverses every one of those pairs. Two supersedes edges from that reading are already applied (phpq over 204c and over a5ea). Retyping the six chain edges to blocked_by while those supersedes edges exist would close a cycle through pm-phpq. Both records are true about different things: the runs really did happen in that order, and the consolidation really did pick phpq as the survivor. The graph cannot express both while supersedes and blocked_by are read into the same execution DAG.

That is a design question for this item and pm-4020c5 to settle, not a data repair: either supersedes stops contributing to the execution DAG, or consolidation lineage needs a kind that is explicitly not an ordering claim. No edges were changed on this cluster pending that decision.

value.text:
Ordering graph re-measured 2026-07-29 at build 2026.7.29. Unchanged in every respect that matters, and this is the expected result.

Ordered node count 2,069, layer count 7, frontier count 1,815, critical path length 6, cycle count 8. The reported critical path is still the same 2026-03-07 duplicate cluster - pm-phpq, pm-204c, pm-iziy, pm-f0e9, pm-mn6w, pm-wjdr, pm-a5ea - wired by the terminal backfill.

Three ordering edges were added this session and all three are blocked_by rows on the dependent item, recording a real prerequisite discovered by measurement rather than inferred from co-occurrence: the graph conformance matrix is blocked on shape-capable corpus generation because its own fixture criterion names shapes no generator can produce; the episode substrate is blocked on the workspace-restore durability defect because episode resets run through restore; the retrieval quality contract is blocked on the gate actually being wired. No ordering edge was manufactured from release cohorts, parent lineage or chronology, which the extraction scan already established as a refusal class at a 67 percent drop rate.

The frontier ratio is therefore still 87.7 percent and the conclusion this item carries stands: the flat ordering graph is an authoring gap, not an extraction gap, and the lever is capture at write time. Every prerequisite recorded this session was written at the moment it was discovered, which is exactly the behaviour the lever needs to make routine.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Mechanical cause identified 2026-07-31, filed as pm-xm0id4. This item's measurement is confirmed and its attribution needs revising.

The measurement holds and has moved slightly: pm graph analyze today reports node_count 2234, edge_count 10167, layer_count 10, critical_path_length 9, and frontier_count 1845 of ordered_node_count 2104, so 87.7 percent of sequenced nodes still have no predecessor. This item's description attributes that to a corpus that records what work belongs to what and almost never what had to happen before what - that is, to under-authoring.

The corpus says otherwise. clearClosedBlockerSignals in src/cli/commands/close.ts:626 removes every dependency row whose kind is blocked_by when an item is closed, unconditionally and regardless of whether the blocker is still open. Counted over every tracked item file: of 1,900 closed items exactly ONE retains a blocked_by row, while 91 of 318 open items hold one. The reverse spelling blocks is untouched by that code path and shows the mirror-image distribution: 189 closed items hold a blocks row against 4 open ones.

That 1-versus-189 split across the same population is not an authoring pattern. Ordering was authored on the blocked endpoint at least as often as on the blocker endpoint, and the close path deleted it every time. Reproduced in an isolated sandbox: an item holding three blocked_by rows to three still-open blockers, plus one related row, retains only the related row after close, and the close history entry lists dependencies among its changed_fields while pm get --at reconstructs the deleted edges.

Two consequences for this item's acceptance criteria. The criterion asking for a stated policy distinguishing items that legitimately have no predecessor from items whose predecessor was never recorded needs a third category: items whose predecessor WAS recorded and was deleted at close. And the criterion asking for recovered sequencing edges from durable evidence cannot be satisfied by writing blocked_by rows onto terminal work, because those rows do not survive the next close - which is the specification pm-ye46ns currently carries.

The predecessor-coverage baseline to trend against is therefore not the frontier count alone but the survival split: blocked_by on 1 of 1,900 closed items versus blocks on 189.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Measurement refresh 2026-07-31 (evening), at HEAD a66797e37. This item's headline numbers are stale in a way that changes what remains to be done, so recording the current figures rather than re-arguing the finding.

                        this item as filed    2026-07-31
  ordered_node_count            1991            2115
  frontier_count (no pred)      1763            1853
  critical_path_length             6               9
  layer_count                      -              10

The frontier ratio barely moved: 88.5 percent then, 87.6 percent now. The critical path grew by half.

That split is the useful part, and it is diagnostic rather than cosmetic. The ordering work done since this item was filed - the outcome-milestone ladder being sequenced against itself on 07-29 and 07-31, plus scattered per-item edges like the one added today - deepened the SPINE without touching the FRONTIER. So the depth complaint in this item's title is now substantially answered while the flatness complaint is not: 1,853 of 2,115 sequenced nodes still have no predecessor, which is 90 more absolute than when the item was filed.

The deepest chain now reads end to end, and it is worth quoting because it is the argument for why the spine work mattered:

  pm-1jrdri -> pm-pbyu -> pm-0z7n -> pm-6apl -> pm-1kxs -> pm-j82fd3 -> pm-9rgaal -> pm-o87av6 -> pm-xp1xsw -> pm-a5w7vv

An uncontracted noun defect, to the grammar ADR, to the alias substrate, to the ops consolidation, to the one-screen agent story, to the grammar milestone, to SDK-complete, to proven scale, to the GA gate. A single contract defect is now provably nine hops upstream of general availability, which is the kind of statement this graph exists to support and could not make at critical path 6.

Consequence for this item's scope, proposed not applied: the remaining work is frontier reduction, not depth. Those are different jobs with different acceptance. Depth is improved by sequencing containers against each other, which is cheap, done, and nearly exhausted. Frontier reduction means authoring a predecessor for individual leaf items, which is the expensive authoring gap - and per the standing finding that pm close deletes blocked_by rows, it cannot be done durably on closed items at all until that deletion is addressed. Splitting the acceptance criteria along that line would let the depth half close on evidence while the frontier half stays open honestly.

One caveat on the acyclic field: analyze now reports acyclic false with cycle_count 8, whereas the lifecycle validate check reports ok with dependency_cycle_count 0 and no sample paths. The two count over different edge-kind sets - lifecycle uses ordering kinds only since PR#554, analyze spans all kinds including deliberately reciprocal related pairs. Not a regression and not introduced by today's edges; noted so a later pass does not read analyze's cycle_count as a lifecycle defect.
